CausalChain: NAFLD -> metabolic/inflammatory stress -> upregulation of FTO (and interplay with ALKBH5/METTL3) -> aberrant m6A demethylation on metabolic/inflammatory mRNAs -> increased mRNA stability and translation -> enhanced lipogenesis and sustained chronic inflammation -> pro-tumorigenic microenvironment formation -> HCC development
Hypothesis: In NAFLD-associated liver carcinogenesis, hepatocyte-specific upregulation of FTO, possibly synergizing with other m6A regulators, induces targeted m6A demethylation of metabolic and inflammatory transcripts. This post-transcriptional reprogramming enhances mRNA stability and translation, driving lipid accumulation and chronic inflammation that remodel the liver microenvironment into a pro-tumorigenic state. By applying advanced single-cell and spatial transcriptomic techniques alongside CRISPR-mediated FTO modulation, we aim to precisely map this causal cascade and establish FTO as a critical and actionable molecular target in NAFLD-driven HCC.
Abstract: We propose that in the progression of NAFLD-associated liver carcinogenesis, metabolic and inflammatory stresses inherent to NAFLD upregulate FTO expression in hepatocytes. Elevated FTO, potentially acting in concert with other m6A modulators such as ALKBH5 and METTL3, drives site-specific m6A demethylation of key metabolic and inflammatory mRNAs. This process stabilizes these transcripts, leading to increased translation of proteins that enhance lipogenesis and chronic inflammatory responses, thereby establishing a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment conducive to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development. To validate this sequential mechanism, we will leverage contemporary methods, including single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene editing, to dissect the temporal and spatial dynamics of FTO activity and its downstream effects in NAFLD livers.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered on increased FTO-mediated m6A demethylation leading to dysregulation of metabolic and inflammatory genes that promote a tumorigenic microenvironment and HCC. The revised hypothesis maintains this core idea but refines it by: (1) explicitly integrating additional m6A regulators (ALKBH5/METTL3) to acknowledge the broader epitranscriptomic context; (2) detailing the molecular outcomes (i.e., mRNA stability, lipogenesis, chronic inflammation) in a stepwise, causal chain; (3) incorporating modern, high-resolution technologies (single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, CRISPR) to enhance experimental rigor and practical implementation; and (4) providing a clearer narrative that directly maps the original causal steps to contemporary investigational strategies.
